name: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

clinicalPearls: Typically affects young adults, often a week or two after a viral prodrome
Causes acute central or paracentral visual loss that is usually bilateral, though the two eyes may be affected sequentially
The fundus shows multiple flat, cream to grey-white placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium and outer retina across the posterior pole
The lesions fade over weeks, leaving pigmentary scarring, and vision commonly recovers as they resolve
Fluorescein angiography shows early blockage (hypofluorescence) and late staining (hyperfluorescence) of the placoid lesions
An important systemic association is cerebral vasculitis, so headache or neurological symptoms warrant urgent investigation
Most cases are self-limiting and observed, with systemic corticosteroids reserved for central nervous system involvement
reference.pathophysiology: The condition is regarded as an inflammatory choroidal vasculitis or choriocapillaris hypoperfusion that secondarily disturbs the overlying retinal pigment epithelium and outer retina, producing the characteristic placoid lesions. It frequently follows a viral illness, suggesting an immune trigger. The same vasculitic process may involve the cerebral circulation, which accounts for the recognised association with meningoencephalitis and stroke.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to identify the placoid lesions
Fluorescein angiography showing early hypofluorescence and late hyperfluorescence
Indocyanine green angiography demonstrating hypofluorescent lesions from choriocapillaris non-perfusion
Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography to document outer retinal disruption
Investigations to exclude syphilis and tuberculosis
Neuroimaging and lumbar puncture if there is headache or neurological signs
redFlags: Headache, meningism or focal neurological signs suggesting cerebral vasculitis or stroke
An atypical or progressive course suggesting serpiginous choroidopathy or an infective placoid disease
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good, with spontaneous visual recovery over several weeks, although some patients are left with residual paracentral scotomata when the fovea has been involved.
pitfalls: Missing associated cerebral vasculitis in a patient reporting headache
Confusing it with serpiginous choroidopathy, which is progressive and recurrent
Failing to exclude syphilis and tuberculosis as infective mimics
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
